newsitem.title: CANADA: Clamor for tax relief mounts in Canada.
newsitem.headline: Clamor for tax relief mounts in Canada.

text.p: If death and taxes are life's two certainties, millions of Canadians believe in a third -- death by taxation.
As Canadian Finance Minister Paul Martin prepares to unveil his annual budget next Tuesday, the chorus for across-the-board tax relief is mounting.

"It's all well and good to present some of the social measures the federal government has been floating, but the best social policy is still to create jobs," said the Certified General Accountants' Association of Canada in a pre-budget release on Thursday.
"Our studies demonstrate that a (C$4 billion/$2.9 billion) tax cut will do just that, raising real gross domestic product by C$5 billion ($3.7 billion) and creating more than 100,000 jobs by 2001."
That appeals to many Canadians who labor under one of the most onerous income tax burdens in the developed world.
Many others, however, view tax cuts as a recipe for the dismantling of Canada's publicly funded social programs -- a mortal blow to universal health care, old-age pensions and welfare allowances.

Canada has the highest personal income taxes among G7 nations and the fourth highest within the Organisation of Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), according to an OECD study. Only Australia, Denmark and New Zealand cut more flesh from their wage earners.
Canada's top marginal tax rate, which clicks in it an annual income of C$62,193 ($45,919), is 54 percent. In contrast, the top U.S. rate is 39.6 percent on those making more than $200,000 a year.
When other taxes -- corporate, sales and pension -- are included, Canada falls to fourth place in the G7, but still ahead of the United States, Britain and Japan.

Canada's high levels of taxation are bleeding the economy dry, said Mitchel Gray, research and policy director for the Canadian Taxpayers Federation, an Alberta-based lobby group claiming 80,000 members.

The Canadian government has raised taxes or eliminated tax benefits more than 20 times since 1994, at a cost of C$7.15 billion ($5.28 billion), or C$979 ($722) a year to each Canadian family, according to the federation.
"A C$4 billion ($2.9 billion) tax cut is needed to stimulate growth in the Canadian economy. Anything else is just not enough," Gray said.
Despite Canada's image as a safe haven for gleeful tax collectors, there is considerable inertia in the Finance Department toward anything resembling a tax cut.
Martin, one of the most conservative and powerful finance ministers in Canadian history, has repeatedly ruled out an across-the-board tax reduction.

"Broad-based tax cuts would have to be paid for either through large increases in borrowing, which would result in higher interest rates and less jobs, or by large cuts in social programs," Martin said at last week's G7 finance ministers' meeting in Berlin.
The tax debate seems a mere sideshow to Martin who is committed to breaking the back of Canada's C$24.3 billion ($17.94 billion) budget deficit.
More than C$13 billion ($9.6 billion) has been chopped from Canada's federal deficit since Martin's Liberal Party took office in late 1993.

Ottawa's unprecedented downsizing has included massive reductions in transfer payments to Canada's 10 provinces, cuts to the civil service and a hike in unemployment insurance premiums and other related taxes.
Martin has pledged to cut the deficit further to C$17 billion ($12.5 billion) in fiscal 1997/98 ending March 31, 1998, and to C$9 billion ($6.6 billion) in 1998/1999.
Economists are convinced the government is at least a year or C$7 billion ($5.1 billion) ahead of its deficit reduction schedule, but most are unwilling to jump on the tax cut locomotive.

The clamor for tax cuts is "simply wrongheaded" because Canada's economy is already responding to the monetary stimulus of declining interest rates, said Tim O'Neill, chief economist with Bank of Montreal.
